This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.\n- humanizer: Use to make AI-sounding text more natural while preserving meaning and voice\n- implementing-react-i18n: Use for React translations, locale resources, language selectors, or stale UI after locale changes\n- improve: Survey any codebase as a senior advisor and produce prioritized, self-contained implementation plans for OTHER models/agents to execute. product direction), or generate handoff plans for another agent to implement.\n- instrumenting-control-planes: Use for observable backend or agent workflows, long-running jobs, retries, recovery, and user-visible failures\n- learning-from-bugs: Use for requested postmortems or reusable lessons from serious architecture, data, security, recovery, or operational failures\n- optimizing-react-next-apps: Use to improve React or Next.js load, compile, render, hydration, bundle, import, or dependency performance\n- receiving-code-review: Use to apply code-review feedback, choose only the skills the task needs\n- verification-before-completion: Use before claiming changed work is complete, fixed, or passing\n- writing-plans: Use to create an implementation plan or durable multi-step handoff\n- writing-skills: Use to create, edit, compress, or verify a reusable agent skill\n- sloptrim:sloptrim: Use when the user wants to humanize text, trim slop, de-AI or de-slop writing, remove AI tells, fix robotic or ChatGPT-sounding prose, or make writing sound human and natural. Also run before delivering a CV, cover letter, email, report, or essay to be sent. Removes 71 documented AI-writing patterns with a local detector, preserves numbers, names and citations, and rebuilds toward a human voice rather than a flat husk. Mode-aware, so it never fabricates voice on factual content.\n- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: \"chart\", \"graph\", \"plot\", \"data viz\", \"visualization\", \"dashboard\", \"analytics\", \"visualize data\", \"categorical colors\", \"sequential / diverging palette\", \"stat tile\", \"sparkline\", \"heatmap\", \"legend\", \"axis\", \"tooltip\", \"chart colors\", \"color by series\".\n- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors (\"from now on when X\", \"each time X\", \"whenever X\", \"before/after X\") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions (\"allow X\", \"add permission\", \"move permission to\"), env vars (\"set X=Y\"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: \"allow npm commands\", \"add bq permission to global settings\", \"move permission to user settings\", \"set DEBUG=true\", \"when claude stops show X\". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.\n- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: \"rebind ctrl+s\", \"add a chord shortcut\", \"change the submit key\", \"customize keybindings\".\n- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.\n- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.\n- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.\n- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). - NEVER EVER EVER delete the `bugdrop-screenshots` branch, locally or remotely. It is protected project history.
- NEVER create a worktree, UNLESS the user has specifically asked for it!
- NEVER delete files unless the user has specifically asked for it. If you think a file is misplaced, unrelated, or stale, that is an entirely separate request — ask first. "Looks unrelated to this task" is not authorization to delete.

- When the user gives a UUID and asks what is going on with it, treat it as an OmniHarness conversation/session lookup: check `[REDACTED]`, starting with the `runs` row for that UUID, then inspect related `workers`, `messages`, `execution_events`, queued messages, and validation/plan records as needed.
- To delete all conversations and associated persisted artifacts, use `scripts/delete-conversations.sh`

Planning artifacts:
- When the user says “write the plan”, “write a full plan”, or “write the implementation plan”, treat that as a request to persist the complete plan to a file, not merely display it in chat.
- If the user gives a path, write the plan there. Otherwise use `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<kebab-case-feature-name>.md`, using the current date and a non-colliding filename.
- The saved file is the canonical full plan. The final response should link to it and summarize the result rather than replacing the file with a chat-only plan.
- This convention applies even when the current message omits the destination because “write the plan” is the project’s established shorthand for creating the plan artifact.
- If the same request explicitly says not to change the workspace or not to create a file, obey that more specific prohibition and ask for a destination when needed.

Testing:
- After any UI/frontend change, always run `pnpm build:interface:web` before considering the work complete.
- When testing the app, use the already-running process if one exists instead of starting another server.
- The normal runner URL is `http://localhost:3050`; the Vite development interface is usually at `http://localhost:5173`.
- Clean up any test sessions/conversations and their associated persisted artifacts before finishing.
- For lifecycle / chaos-style regressions (reconnect, restart, FK-on-delete, plan-review leftover state), use `pnpm test:lifecycle`. Scenarios live under `tests/lifecycle/scenarios/` and drive the control plane via HTTP/SSE — no Chromium. To debug a specific reported bug, mirror it as a new scenario file.
- Read `docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md` before adding new server-side state transitions. It is the spec all new code is held to.
- Worker conversation content (direct-control and supervisor-driven worker turns) lives in the unified worker stream — one append-only JSONL per worker at `app-data/run-data/<runId>/<workerId>.jsonl`. Persist new worker content through `appendWorkerEntry` in `src/server/workers/output-store.ts`; render it through `WorkerEntriesManager` and the `entries` prop on `Terminal`. Do NOT add a parallel persistence layer (a sibling JSONL, a new `messages.kind`, an in-memory cache that the frontend reconciles against the stream). See `docs/architecture/worker-conversation-stream.md`.

Lifecycle observability rules (full doc: `docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md`):
- Every server-side decision (spawn, reattach, recreate, give up, refuse, delete, fail) emits a typed named event via `emitNamedEvent` from `@/server/events/named-events`. Silent early returns and bare `catch {}` are bugs.
- User-relevant failures additionally emit `error.surfaced` with a stable `code` (typed union in `named-events.ts`), `surface`, and at least one relevant subject id such as `runId`/`workerId`/`conversationId`/`accountId`. Never funnel through a blanket wrapper in `api-errors.ts`.
- All SSE frames carry an `id:`. Clients reconnect with `Last-Event-ID`; the server replays from the ring buffer or emits `stream.resync_required`. Snapshot bootstrap is `GET /api/events?snapshot=1` (anchor id in the `x-omni-last-event-id` response header).
- Dev-only event log: `GET /api/events/log?since=<id>&runId=<id>` returns the ring buffer as JSON. Use this when triaging "X didn't happen" bug reports — if the event isn't there, the server didn't do the thing, and the next step is finding the silent branch.
- Chaos is a client-side concern. Never add fault-injection code paths to server code.

Frontend i18n:
- EVERY user-facing frontend string MUST live in `shared/locales/*.json` and be rendered with the `t()` function from `@/lib/i18n`.
- NEVER hardcode user-facing JSX text, button labels, dialog titles, aria-labels, titles, placeholders, empty states, status labels, help text, error fallback text, or visible option labels directly in components.
- For every new user-facing string, add the key to `shared/locales/en.json` and every other locale file in `shared/locales/` in the same change. Use stable dotted keys like `settings.runtime.recovery` or `conversation.sidebar.search`.
- Components that render translated strings and need to update when the language changes MUST subscribe to the i18n manager by calling `useI18nSnapshot()` from `@/lib/i18n`; then render text with the existing `t("key", params?)` function. The hook is only for re-rendering; `t()` is the translation API.
- Non-React modules that produce user-visible text must still use `t("key", params?)` at the boundary where text is produced. Protocol values, storage keys, API paths, CSS classes, model ids, and database values are not translation keys unless they are displayed as copy.
- Do not pass translated strings through transactions or persist translated UI copy. Store stable ids/values and translate at render time.

React Best Practices:
- MutableRefObject is deprecated in React; use RefObject instead.
- NEVER use require() to import modules. Use import instead.
- ALWAYS centralize all state in global single source of truth Manager classes. Components/listeners subscribe to updates from Managers and use Manager methods to update data.
- Always implement a custom data manager for any data structure. NEVER use separate state variables and arrays as the source of truth.
- NEVER send data around in transactions.
- Avoid using useEffect() to update state. Prefer useCallback() or Manager methods for explicit state transitions.
- Avoid callback hell, race conditions, and infinite loops.
- NEVER store string literals or UI settings for the frontend in the .env file. Use literals in files, inline arrays, or .json files instead.
- When debugging React: if a fix did not work, think hard about whether this is a race condition. Race conditions are common in React.

      "name": "ScheduleWakeup",
      "description": "Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.\n\nDo NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.\n\nPass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.\n\nSet `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report (\"no change\", \"still waiting\", \"quiet hold\"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).\n\n## Picking delaySeconds\n\nThis session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)\n\nMatch the delay to what you're actually waiting for:\n\n- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.\n- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.\n- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.\n\nDon't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.\n\n## The reason field\n\nOne short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. \"watching CI run\" beats \"waiting.\" The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.\n",

    {
      "name": "Workflow",
      "description": "Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.\n\nONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:\n- The user included the keyword \"ultracode\" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).\n- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.\n- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words (\"use a workflow\", \"run a workflow\", \"fan out agents\", \"orchestrate this with subagents\"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.\n- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.\n- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.\n\nFor any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with \"use a workflow\" in a future message to skip the ask.\n\nEvery script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.\n\nThe canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:\n  export const meta = {\n    name: 'review-changes',\n    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',\n    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],\n  }\n  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]\n  const results = await pipeline(\n    DIMENSIONS,\n    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),\n    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>\n      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})\n        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))\n    ))\n  )\n  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)\n  return { confirmed }\n  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.\n\nBefore writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.\n\nThis session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with \"Dynamic workflow size\" in /config.",

Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.\n\nONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:\n- The user included the keyword \"ultracode\" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).\n- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.\n- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words (\"use a workflow\", \"run a workflow\", \"fan out agents\", \"orchestrate this with subagents\"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.\n- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.\n- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.\n\nFor any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with \"use a workflow\" in a future message to skip the ask.\n\nEvery script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.\n\nThe canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:\n  export const meta = {\n    name: 'review-changes',\n    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',\n    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],\n  }\n  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]\n  const results = await pipeline(\n    DIMENSIONS,\n    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),\n    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>\n      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})\n        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))\n    ))\n  )\n  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)\n  return { confirmed }\n  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.\n\nBefore writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.\n\nThis session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with \"Dynamic workflow size\" in /config.",

29	  advanceWorkerTurnGeneration,
30	  beginConversationRecoveryPreemption,
31	  finishConversationRecoveryPreemption,
32	  isWorkerTurnAbortedError,
33	  isWorkerTurnSupersededError,
34	  isWorkerTurnGenerationCurrent,
35	  runConversationMutation,
36	  runWorkerTurn,
37	  trackConversationBackgroundTask,
38	} from "./worker-turn-gate";
39	import { buildDirectWorkerPrompt } from "./direct-worker-prompt";
40	import { assertRunNotHandoffFenced } from "@/server/handoff/fence";
41	import {
42	  isProviderSessionDiagnosticErrorMessage,
43	  userFacingProviderSessionErrorMessage,
44	} from "@/server/workers/session-recovery";
45	import { recreateWorkerFromTranscript } from "@/server/workers/provider-session-recovery";
46	
47	type RunRecord = typeof runs.$inferSelect;
48	type WorkerRecord = typeof workers.$inferSelect;
49	type QueuedRecord = typeof queuedConversationMessages.$inferSelect;
50	
51	export type InterruptSource = "escape" | "drawer" | "api";
52	
53	export interface InterruptResult {
54	  ok: true;
55	  message?: ReturnType<typeof serializeMessageRecord>;
56	  queuedMessage: ReturnType<typeof serializeQueuedConversationMessage>;
57	  interruption: {
58	    status: "delivering" | "deferred";
59	    workerId: string;
60	    cancelDurationMs: number;
61	  };
62	}
63	
64	const RECOVERY_IN_PROGRESS_MESSAGE = "Worker recovery in progress.";
65	const RECOVERY_SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000;
66	
67	function workerTurnSupersededError(workerId: string) {
68	  return new Error(`Worker turn was superseded by a newer worker turn: ${workerId}`);
69	}
70	
71	async function waitForRecoverySettlement(args: {
72	  runId: string;
73	  workerId: string;
74	  generation: number;
75	}) {
76	  const deadline = Date.now() + RECOVERY_SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS;
77	  while (true) {
78	    if (!await isWorkerTurnGenerationCurrent(args.workerId, args.generation)) {
79	      throw workerTurnSupersededError(args.workerId);
80	    }
81	    const activeIncident = await db.select({ id: recoveryIncidents.id })
82	      .from(recoveryIncidents)
83	      .where(and(
84	        eq(recoveryIncidents.runId, args.runId),
85	        eq(recoveryIncidents.workerId, args.workerId),
86	        inArray(recoveryIncidents.status, ["open", "recovering"]),
87	      ))
88	      .get();
89	    if (!activeIncident) return;
90	    if (Date.now() >= deadline) {
91	      throw new Error(`Worker recovery did not finish within ${RECOVERY_SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS / 1_000} seconds.`);
92	    }
93	    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
94	  }
95	}
96	
97	function refusal(status: number, message: string) {
98	  return Object.assign(new Error(message), { status });
99	}
100	
101	async function queuedRowStatus(messageId: string) {
102	  const record = await db
103	    .select({ status: queuedConversationMessages.status })
104	    .from(queuedConversationMessages)
105	    .where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, messageId))
106	    .get();
107	  return record?.status ?? null;
108	}
109	
110	function timestampMs(value: Date | string | number | null | undefined) {
111	  if (value instanceof Date) {
112	    return value.getTime();
113	  }
114	  const parsed = new Date(value ?? 0).getTime();
115	  return Number.isFinite(parsed) ? parsed : 0;
116	}
117	
118	async function loadRun(runId: string): Promise<RunRecord> {
119	  const run = await db.select().from(runs).where(eq(runs.id, runId)).get();
120	  if (!run) {
121	    throw refusal(404, "Conversation not found");
122	  }
123	  return run;
124	}
125	
126	async function loadQueuedRecord(runId: string, messageId: string): Promise<QueuedRecord> {
127	  const record = await db
128	    .select()
129	    .from(queuedConversationMessages)
130	    .where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, messageId))
131	    .get();
132	  if (!record || record.runId !== runId) {
133	    throw refusal(404, "Queued message not found");
134	  }
135	  if (record.status === "delivered") {
136	    throw refusal(409, "Queued message was already delivered");
137	  }
138	  if (record.status === "cancelled") {
139	    throw refusal(409, "Queued message was cancelled");
140	  }
141	  return record;
142	}
143	
144	async function selectOldestPendingRecord(runId: string): Promise<QueuedRecord> {
145	  const records = await db
146	    .select()
147	    .from(queuedConversationMessages)
148	    .where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.runId, runId))
149	    .orderBy(asc(queuedConversationMessages.createdAt), asc(queuedConversationMessages.id));
150	  const pending = records.find((record) => record.status === "pending");
151	  if (!pending) {
152	    emitNamedEvent({
153	      kind: "queue.interrupt_refused",
154	      runId,
155	      workerId: null,
156	      queuedMessageId: null,
157	      reason: "no_user_intent",
158	      source: "escape",
159	    });
160	    throw refusal(409, "No queued message to interrupt");
161	  }
162	  return pending;
163	}
164	
165	async function resolveInterruptWorker(run: RunRecord, record: QueuedRecord): Promise<WorkerRecord | null> {
166	  const targetWorker = record.targetWorkerId
167	    ? await db.select().from(workers).where(eq(workers.id, record.targetWorkerId)).get()
168	    : null;
169	  if (targetWorker && targetWorker.runId === run.id && !isCancelledWorkerStatus(targetWorker.status)) {
170	    return targetWorker;
171	  }
172	  const latest = await getLatestRunWorker(run.id, record.targetWorkerId);
173	  if (latest && latest.runId === run.id && !isCancelledWorkerStatus(latest.status)) {
174	    return latest;
175	  }
176	  return null;
177	}
178	
179	/**
180	 * Core control-plane flow shared by every interrupt entry point:
181	 * cancel the active turn, advance the worker turn fence into a delivery-safe
182	 * state, then deliver exactly one queued user message through the unified
183	 * worker stream. Emits named + execution events for every decision.
184	 */
185	async function interruptAndDeliver(args: {
186	  run: RunRecord;
187	  record: QueuedRecord;
188	  source: InterruptSource;
189	}): Promise<InterruptResult> {
190	  const { run, record, source } = args;
191	  const runId = run.id;
192	  const requestedAt = Date.now();
193	
194	  emitNamedEvent({
195	    kind: "queue.interrupt_requested",
196	    runId,
197	    workerId: record.targetWorkerId ?? null,
198	    queuedMessageId: record.id,
199	    source,
200	  });
201	  await recordExecutionEvent({
202	    runId,
203	    workerId: record.targetWorkerId ?? null,
204	    eventType: "queued_message_interrupt_requested",
205	    details: {
206	      summary: "User requested an interrupt-and-send for a queued message.",
207	      queuedMessageId: record.id,
208	      source,
209	    },
210	  });
211	
212	  const worker = await resolveInterruptWorker(run, record);
213	  if (!worker) {
214	    emitNamedEvent({
215	      kind: "queue.interrupt_refused",
216	      runId,
217	      workerId: record.targetWorkerId ?? null,
218	      queuedMessageId: record.id,
219	      reason: "worker_missing",
220	      source,
221	    });
222	    emitNamedEvent({
223	      kind: "error.surfaced",
224	      code: "queue.interrupt.refused",
225	      message: "No active worker is available to interrupt.",
226	      surface: "toast",
227	      runId,
228	    });
229	    throw refusal(409, "No active worker is available to interrupt");
230	  }
231	
232	  // Steer is cancel-and-replace, and it must be instant. Two rules make it so:
233	  //
234	  //   1. The local abort is authoritative. Tripping the running turn's signal
235	  //      tears down its in-flight request here and now; it needs no cooperation
236	  //      from an agent that may be wedged.
237	  //   2. `session/cancel` is best-effort. It tells the agent to stop the work it
238	  //      is doing, which is worth sending, but awaiting it put a possibly
239	  //      unbounded round trip on the user's critical path — a wedged adapter
240	  //      used to block the steer button indefinitely, and a failed cancel
241	  //      refused the steer outright with a 502.
242	  const cancelStartedAt = Date.now();
243	  const abortedLiveTurn = abortWorkerTurn(worker.id, "user steer");
244	  const agentCancelSettled = Promise.resolve()
245	    .then(() => cancelAgentTurn(worker.id))
246	    .then(() => undefined)
247	    .catch(async (error) => {
248	      await recordExecutionEvent({
249	        runId,
250	        workerId: worker.id,
251	        eventType: "queued_message_interrupt_cancel_best_effort_failed",
252	        details: {
253	          summary: `Agent-side cancel for ${worker.id} failed after the turn was already aborted locally.`,
254	          queuedMessageId: record.id,
255	          error: errorMessage(error),
256	          source,
257	        },
258	      }).catch(() => undefined);
259	    });
260	  const cancelDurationMs = Date.now() - cancelStartedAt;
261	
262	  // Advance the fence and reset persisted worker state into a delivery-safe
263	  // shape in one mutation so immediate delivery cannot observe stale `working`.
264	  const cancelledAt = new Date();
265	  const generation = await advanceWorkerTurnGeneration(worker.id, {
266	    status: "idle",
267	    clearCurrentText: true,
268	    updatedAt: cancelledAt,
269	  });
270	
271	  emitNamedEvent({
272	    kind: "queue.interrupt_cancelled_turn",
273	    runId,
274	    workerId: worker.id,
275	    queuedMessageId: record.id,
276	    cancelDurationMs,
277	    source,
278	  });
279	  await recordExecutionEvent({
280	    runId,
281	    workerId: worker.id,
282	    eventType: "queued_message_turn_cancelled",
283	    details: {
284	      summary: `Interrupted the active turn for ${worker.id}.`,
285	      queuedMessageId: record.id,
286	      cancelDurationMs,
287	      abortedLiveTurn,
288	      source,
289	    },
290	  });
291	
292	  // Mark the row delivering and move the run back into an active state.
293	  const startedAt = new Date();
294	  await db.update(queuedConversationMessages).set({
295	    action: "steer",
296	    targetWorkerId: worker.id,
297	    status: "delivering",
298	    lastError: null,
299	    updatedAt: startedAt,
300	  }).where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, record.id));
301	  await db.update(runs).set({
302	    status: run.mode === "planning" ? "working" : "running",
303	    failedAt: null,
304	    lastError: null,
305	    updatedAt: startedAt,
306	  }).where(eq(runs.id, runId));
307	
308	  emitNamedEvent({
309	    kind: "queue.interrupt_delivery_started",
310	    runId,
311	    workerId: worker.id,
312	    queuedMessageId: record.id,
313	    totalInterruptLatencyMs: Date.now() - requestedAt,
314	    source,
315	  });
316	  notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
317	
318	  const normalizedAttachments = normalizeChatAttachments(
319	    record.attachmentsJson ? JSON.parse(record.attachmentsJson) : [],
320	  );
321	  const workerContent = appendAttachmentContext(record.content, normalizedAttachments, {
322	    resolvePath: (storagePath) => getAppDataPath(storagePath),
323	    imagesInlined: true,
324	  });
325	
326	  const userMessage = {
327	    id: record.id,
328	    runId,
329	    role: "user" as const,
330	    kind: "checkpoint" as const,
331	    content: record.content,
332	    attachmentsJson: record.attachmentsJson,
333	    createdAt: startedAt,
334	  };
335	
336	  trackConversationBackgroundTask(
337	    deliverInterruptedQueuedMessage({
338	      run,
339	      worker,
340	      record,
341	      userMessage,
342	      workerContent,
343	      attachments: normalizedAttachments,
344	      generation,
345	      agentCancelSettled,
346	      source,
347	      requestedAt,
348	    }).catch((error) => {
349	      if (isWorkerTurnSupersededError(error) || isWorkerTurnAbortedError(error)) {
350	        return;
351	      }
352	      console.error("Queued message interrupt delivery failed:", error);
353	    }),
354	    { runId },
355	  );
356	
357	  return {
358	    ok: true,
359	    message: serializeMessageRecord(userMessage),
360	    queuedMessage: serializeQueuedConversationMessage({
361	      ...record,
362	      action: "steer",
363	      targetWorkerId: worker.id,
364	      status: "delivering",
365	      lastError: null,
366	      updatedAt: startedAt,
367	      deliveredAt: null,
368	    }),
369	    interruption: {
370	      status: "delivering",
371	      workerId: worker.id,
372	      cancelDurationMs,
373	    },
374	  };
375	}
376	
377	async function deliverInterruptedQueuedMessage(args: {
378	  run: RunRecord;
379	  worker: WorkerRecord;
380	  record: QueuedRecord;
381	  userMessage: {
382	    id: string;
383	    runId: string;
384	    role: "user";
385	    kind: "checkpoint";
386	    content: string;
387	    attachmentsJson: string | null;
388	    createdAt: Date;
389	  };
390	  workerContent: string;
391	  attachments: ChatAttachment[];
392	  generation: number;
393	  agentCancelSettled: Promise<void>;
394	  source: InterruptSource;
395	  requestedAt: number;
396	}) {
397	  const { run, worker, record, userMessage, workerContent, attachments, generation, agentCancelSettled, source, requestedAt } = args;
398	  const runId = run.id;
399	
400	  /**
401	   * A stale terminal write must never overwrite a newer interrupt delivery or a
402	   * row the user cancelled mid-flight, so every terminal mutation re-checks the
403	   * row status and the turn fence.
404	   *
405	   * Bailing out used to just `return`, which left the row in `delivering`
406	   * forever — a state nothing else ever resolves. So a superseded delivery is
407	   * released here instead:
408	   *
409	   * - `appended: false` — nothing was written yet, so the row goes back to
410	   *   `pending`: the message is still queued, visible, and retryable.
411	   * - `appended: true` — the message is already in the transcript and its id is
412	   *   the primary key of the `messages` row, so re-delivering it would collide.
413	   *   The row is closed as delivered and the supersede is recorded.
414	   */
415	  const releaseSupersededRow = async (appended: boolean) => {
416	    if (await queuedRowStatus(record.id) !== "delivering") {
417	      return;
418	    }
419	    const now = new Date();
420	    await db.update(queuedConversationMessages).set({
421	      status: appended ? "delivered" : "pending",
422	      lastError: null,
423	      updatedAt: now,
424	      ...(appended ? { deliveredAt: now } : {}),
425	    }).where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, record.id));
426	    await recordExecutionEvent({
427	      runId,
428	      workerId: worker.id,
429	      eventType: "queued_message_interrupt_superseded",
430	      details: {
431	        summary: appended
432	          ? `A newer turn took over after ${worker.id} already received this message.`
433	          : `Requeued the message for ${worker.id} because a newer turn took over before it was sent.`,
434	        queuedMessageId: record.id,
435	        appendedToTranscript: appended,
436	        source,
437	      },
438	    });
439	  };
440	
441	  const isStillCurrent = async (appended = false) => {
442	    if (await queuedRowStatus(record.id) !== "delivering") {
443	      return false;
444	    }
445	    if (await isWorkerTurnGenerationCurrent(worker.id, generation)) {
446	      return true;
447	    }
448	    await releaseSupersededRow(appended);
449	    return false;
450	  };
451	
452	  let appendedToTranscript = false;
453	
454	  try {
455	    // The API has already returned, so waiting here does not hold up the UI.
456	    // Starting the replacement request before the provider confirms the old
457	    // cancellation lets the late cancel or late output hit the new turn.
458	    await agentCancelSettled;
459	    await runWorkerTurn(worker.id, async () => {
460	      if (!(await isStillCurrent())) {
461	        notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
462	        return;
463	      }
464	
465	      const workerClaimed = await db.update(workers).set({
466	        status: "working",
467	        updatedAt: new Date(),
468	      }).where(and(
469	        eq(workers.id, worker.id),
470	        eq(workers.turnGeneration, generation),
471	      )).returning({ id: workers.id }).get();
472	      if (!workerClaimed) {
473	        await releaseSupersededRow(false);
474	        return;
475	      }
476	
477	      const deliveredAt = new Date();
478	      await appendUserInputOnDelivery({
479	        id: userMessage.id,
480	        runId,
481	        workerId: worker.id,
482	        text: record.content,
483	        deliveredAt,
484	        attachments: attachments.map((attachment) => ({
485	          id: attachment.id,
486	          filename: attachment.name,
487	          mimeType: attachment.mimeType,
488	          sizeBytes: attachment.size,
489	          storagePath: attachment.storagePath,
490	        })),
491	        expectedTurnGeneration: generation,
492	      });
493	      if (!(await isStillCurrent())) {
494	        notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
495	        return;
496	      }
497	      await db.insert(messages).values(userMessage);
498	      appendedToTranscript = true;
499	      notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
500	
501	      if (!(await isStillCurrent(true))) {
502	        notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
503	        return;
504	      }
505	
506	      const workerPrompt = run.mode === "direct" || run.mode === "commit"
507	        ? buildDirectWorkerPrompt(workerContent)
508	        : workerContent;
509	      const imageAttachments = resolveImageAttachments(attachments, getAppDataPath);
510	      let response;
511	      try {
512	        response = imageAttachments.length
513	          ? await askAgent(worker.id, workerPrompt, imageAttachments)
514	          : await askAgent(worker.id, workerPrompt);
515	      } catch (error) {
516	        if (!isProviderSessionDiagnosticErrorMessage(errorMessage(error))) {
517	          throw error;
518	        }
519	
520	        const currentWorker = await db.select().from(workers).where(eq(workers.id, worker.id)).get();
521	        const recreated = await recreateWorkerFromTranscript({
522	          run,
523	          worker: currentWorker ?? worker,
524	          nextUserPrompt: workerPrompt,
525	          source: "steer",
526	          reason: "provider_session_diagnostic_after_steer",
527	          expectedTurnGeneration: generation,
528	        });
529	        await db.update(workers).set({
530	          status: "working",
531	          updatedAt: new Date(),
532	        }).where(and(
533	          eq(workers.id, worker.id),
534	          eq(workers.turnGeneration, generation),
535	        ));
536	        response = imageAttachments.length
537	          ? await askAgent(worker.id, recreated.replayPrompt, imageAttachments)
538	          : await askAgent(worker.id, recreated.replayPrompt);
539	      }
540	      const finishedAt = new Date();
541	
542	      // Before any terminal persistence, confirm a newer interrupt has not
543	      // superseded this delivery and the row was not cancelled.
544	      if (!(await isStillCurrent(true))) {
545	        notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
546	        return;
547	      }
548	
549	      await persistDeliveredWorkerResponse({
550	        run: { id: runId, mode: run.mode },
551	        workerId: worker.id,
552	        response,
553	        deliveredAt: finishedAt,
554	        userInputEntryId: userMessage.id,
555	        expectedTurnGeneration: generation,
556	      });
557	
558	      if (!(await isStillCurrent(true))) {
559	        notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
560	        return;
561	      }
562	
563	      await db.update(queuedConversationMessages).set({
564	        status: "delivered",
565	        lastError: null,
566	        updatedAt: finishedAt,
567	        deliveredAt: finishedAt,
568	      }).where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, record.id));
569	      await recordExecutionEvent({
570	        runId,
571	        workerId: worker.id,
572	        eventType: "queued_message_interrupt_delivered",
573	        details: {
574	          summary: `Delivered interrupted queued message to ${worker.id}.`,
575	          queuedMessageId: record.id,
576	          source,
577	        },
578	      });
579	      emitNamedEvent({
580	        kind: "queue.interrupt_delivery_finished",
581	        runId,
582	        workerId: worker.id,
583	        queuedMessageId: record.id,
584	        totalInterruptLatencyMs: Date.now() - requestedAt,
585	        source,
586	      });
587	      notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
588	    });
589	  } catch (error) {
590	    // A superseded turn lost a race; an aborted turn was stopped on purpose.
591	    // Neither is a delivery failure, and reporting them as one puts a red error
592	    // on the conversation every time the user presses stop or steers again.
593	    if (isWorkerTurnSupersededError(error) || isWorkerTurnAbortedError(error)) {
594	      await releaseSupersededRow(appendedToTranscript);
595	      notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
596	      return;
597	    }
598	    await handleInterruptDeliveryError({ run, worker, record, userMessage, error, generation, source, requestedAt });
599	  }
600	}
601	
602	async function handleInterruptDeliveryError(args: {
603	  run: RunRecord;
604	  worker: WorkerRecord;
605	  record: QueuedRecord;
606	  userMessage: { id: string; createdAt: Date };
607	  error: unknown;
608	  generation: number;
609	  source: InterruptSource;
610	  requestedAt: number;
611	}) {
612	  const { run, worker, record, userMessage, error, generation, source, requestedAt } = args;
613	  const runId = run.id;
614	  const failedAt = new Date();
615	
616	  // A late failure from an interrupted (older) turn or a row the user cancelled
617	  // must not flip queue state.
618	  if (await queuedRowStatus(record.id) !== "delivering") {
619	    notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
620	    return;
621	  }
622	  if (!(await isWorkerTurnGenerationCurrent(worker.id, generation))) {
623	    const currentRecord = await db
624	      .select({ updatedAt: queuedConversationMessages.updatedAt })
625	      .from(queuedConversationMessages)
626	      .where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, record.id))
627	      .get();
628	    if (timestampMs(currentRecord?.updatedAt) > timestampMs(userMessage.createdAt)) {
629	      notifyEventStreamSubscribers();
630	      return;
631	    }
632	  }
633	
634	  const rawErrorMessage = errorMessage(error);
635	  const surfacedErrorMessage = userFacingProviderSessionErrorMessage(rawErrorMessage);
636	  const busy = isAgentBusyError(error);
637	  const missingAgent = isAgentNotFoundError(error);
638	  await db.update(queuedConversationMessages).set({
639	    status: busy ? "pending" : "failed",
640	    lastError: missingAgent ? RECOVERY_IN_PROGRESS_MESSAGE : surfacedErrorMessage,
641	    updatedAt: failedAt,
642	  }).where(eq(queuedConversationMessages.id, record.id));
643	
644	  // The persisted worker outlived its in-memory runtime agent. That is a
645	  // normal recovery trigger after a restart, not a user-facing delivery
646	  // failure. Keep the internal breadcrumb, recover/requeue the message, and
647	  // let the recovery lifecycle events describe what happened.
648	  if (missingAgent) {
649	    await recordExecutionEvent({
650	      runId,
651	      workerId: worker.id,
652	      eventType: "queued_message_recovery_blocked",
653	      details: {
654	        summary: `Queued message ${record.id} is waiting for ${worker.id} to be recovered.`,
655	        queuedMessageId: record.id,
656	        error: rawErrorMessage,
657	        source,
658	      },
659	    });
660	    // The checkpoint row was inserted before the failed ask. The worker stream
661	    // can deduplicate its stable id, but the relational row cannot, so remove
662	    // it before the recovered queue delivery inserts that same id again.
663	    await db.delete(messages).where(eq(messages.id, userMessage.id));
664	    try {
665	      const recovery = await reconcileRunRecovery({
666	        runId,
667	        liveAgents: [],
668	        source: "queued-message-interrupt",
669	      });
670	      if (recovery.action === "none") {
671	        // Another reconciliation may own the spawn. Its incident settles only
672	        // after all queue rewrites are complete, which prevents its final
673	        // requeue from racing this delivery back to pending.

829	async function interruptAndSendQueuedConversationMessageNowUnlocked(params: {
830	  runId: string;
831	  messageId: string;
832	  source?: InterruptSource;
833	}): Promise<InterruptResult> {
834	  await assertRunNotHandoffFenced(params.runId);
835	  const run = await loadRun(params.runId);
836	  const record = await loadQueuedRecord(params.runId, params.messageId);
837	  return interruptAndDeliver({ run, record, source: params.source ?? "drawer" });
838	}
839	
840	/**
841	 * A retry/edit holds the conversation mutex for its whole replayed provider
842	 * turn (`recoverRun` awaits the turn inline). An interrupt that queued behind
843	 * it used to wait out that entire turn and surface as HTTP 524 at the proxy.
844	 * Bumping the recovery epoch aborts the holder's turn synchronously via its
845	 * ambient AbortSignal, so the mutex frees in milliseconds instead of minutes —
846	 * which is what "interrupt" means from the user's side.
847	 */
848	export async function preemptRecoveryForInterrupt<T>(runId: string, task: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
849	  const epoch = beginConversationRecoveryPreemption(runId, "user steer");
850	  try {
851	    return await runConversationMutation(runId, task);
852	  } finally {
853	    finishConversationRecoveryPreemption(runId, epoch);
854	  }
855	}
856	
857	export function interruptAndSendQueuedConversationMessageNow(args: Parameters<typeof interruptAndSendQueuedConversationMessageNowUnlocked>[0]) {
858	  return preemptRecoveryForInterrupt(args.runId, () => interruptAndSendQueuedConversationMessageNowUnlocked(args));
859	}
860	
861	async function interruptAndSendNextQueuedConversationMessageUnlocked(params: {
862	  runId: string;
863	  source?: InterruptSource;
864	}): Promise<InterruptResult> {
865	  await assertRunNotHandoffFenced(params.runId);
866	  const run = await loadRun(params.runId);
867	  const record = await selectOldestPendingRecord(params.runId);
868	  return interruptAndDeliver({ run, record, source: params.source ?? "escape" });
869	}
870	
871	export function interruptAndSendNextQueuedConversationMessage(args: Parameters<typeof interruptAndSendNextQueuedConversationMessageUnlocked>[0]) {
872	  return preemptRecoveryForInterrupt(args.runId, () => interruptAndSendNextQueuedConversationMessageUnlocked(args));
873	}
874	
875	async function interruptWithDraftMessageUnlocked(params: {
876	  runId: string;
877	  content: string;
878	  attachments?: ChatAttachment[];
879	  targetWorkerId?: string | null;
880	  source?: InterruptSource;
881	  clientMessageId?: string | null;
882	  operationFingerprint?: string | null;
883	}): Promise<InterruptResult> {
884	  await assertRunNotHandoffFenced(params.runId);
885	  const run = await loadRun(params.runId);
886	  const trimmed = params.content.trim();
887	  const normalizedAttachments = normalizeChatAttachments(params.attachments ?? []);
888	  if (!trimmed && normalizedAttachments.length === 0) {
889	    emitNamedEvent({
890	      kind: "queue.interrupt_refused",
891	      runId: params.runId,
892	      workerId: params.targetWorkerId ?? null,
893	      queuedMessageId: null,
894	      reason: "no_user_intent",
895	      source: params.source ?? "escape",
896	    });
897	    throw refusal(400, "Message content or attachment is required");
898	  }
899	
900	  // Persist the draft as exactly one queued row, then deliver that same id.
901	  const created = await createQueuedConversationMessage({
902	    runId: params.runId,
903	    targetWorkerId: params.targetWorkerId ?? null,
904	    action: "steer",
905	    content: params.content,
906	    attachments: normalizedAttachments,
907	    clientMessageId: params.clientMessageId,
908	    operationFingerprint: params.operationFingerprint,
909	  });
910	  const record = await loadQueuedRecord(params.runId, created.id);
911	  return interruptAndDeliver({ run, record, source: params.source ?? "escape" });
912	}
913	
914	export function interruptWithDraftMessage(args: Parameters<typeof interruptWithDraftMessageUnlocked>[0]) {
915	  return preemptRecoveryForInterrupt(args.runId, () => interruptWithDraftMessageUnlocked(args));

## Claude · 2026-10-06T15:52:46.398Z

The model never saw your messages. OmniHarness put them in the chat view, then held them in an internal queue that stopped moving at 15:31. Nothing reached Claude, so it carried on with its own work and only reacted to background-task notifications.

## What happened in fc8d9cb681ef

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 15:31:35 | You sent "we should also focus on making our AI run as fast…" while the worker was busy, so it went through the interrupt-and-send path. |
| 15:31:35 | OmniHarness aborted the turn on its own side and sent `session/cancel`, but Claude's turn kept running. The bridge marked the agent idle anyway and sent your message as a new prompt. Claude Code folded it into the turn that was still running (its transcript logs `absorbed_mid_turn`) and replied at 15:32:52. |
| after that | The request carrying that message never got a final answer. Its queued row is still `delivering`. The bridge sends a keep-alive every few seconds, so the runner keeps waiting with no timeout. |
| 15:33:57, 15:46:06, 15:47:38 | "can you run FASTER", the hyperframes message with `delegation-plan.md`, and "did you ignore my last message?" Each was written to the chat stream, so it looked sent, and then waited behind the stuck request in the per-worker queue (`runWorkerTurn`). All three are still `delivering` in `messages`. |
| meanwhile | Background-task notifications start turns from inside Claude Code without going through that queue. They kept arriving (device checklist done, production baseline done), so the model kept working and replying as if you'd said nothing. |

Evidence:
- Claude Code's own transcript (`~/.claude/projects/-Users-masterman-NLP-cloudcaptions/ba5f8bb1-….jsonl`) has no record of any of the three messages, only `<task-notification>` inputs after 15:31.
- The OmniHarness event log shows no worker activity or queue event when you sent at 15:46:06 or 15:47:38.

One link is inferred rather than observed: I didn't catch the stuck request directly. But `delivering` is the only state the interrupt code leaves while it is still waiting on that request, and the bridge reports nothing in flight.

## The bugs
1. **The bridge can send a new prompt over one that hasn't finished.** `cancelAgentTurn` in `src/server/agent-runtime/manager.ts:2384` flips the agent to `idle` as soon as the cancel is sent, even when the old prompt hasn't finished. The next `askAgent` passes the busy check, Claude absorbs it into the running turn, and the second request is never answered. The two overlapping requests also overwrite each other's status on the same agent record.
2. **One stuck request blocks the conversation silently and forever.** `runWorkerTurn` has no watchdog. A request still open after the provider has gone idle never fails, and nothing emits `error.surfaced`, which breaks the lifecycle-observability rules in agents.md.
3. **The UI says "sent" too early.** The message is added to the chat stream before it is delivered, so you see no queued or stuck indicator.

On "we broke something recently": this conversation's signature (messages stuck in `delivering`) appears only here and only today. The interrupt flow dates from Sep 5 (`371c9fa6`) and the Claude adapter (0.81.0) from Sep 23, so I can't point to a specific recent commit. If other conversations show the same symptom, send their IDs and I'll check whether it's the same cause.

## Unsticking this conversation
The stuck request lives only in the runner's memory. Restarting the runner, or pressing Stop on the worker, should clear it. Then resend the hyperframes message: the three stuck ones may be dropped as out of date rather than delivered.

I haven't changed anything. If you want, I'll fix it:
- In the bridge, keep the agent busy until the old prompt has actually finished before sending a steer.
- In the runner, fail any request that is still open after the provider reports the turn ended, and surface that as an error.
- Add a `tests/lifecycle` scenario that reproduces this exact steer sequence.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T15:53:37.604Z

I need to make sure the bridge manager doesn't flip state to idle while a prompt is still in flight, and that the busy check accounts for that. There's also a race in the steer path where the interrupt delivery waits for cancellation to settle before sending a new prompt, but the bridge could still reject with a 409 if the old prompt hasn't fully finished.

The timing suggests the old turn was still running when the queued prompt was marked absorbed, so I need to decide whether to wait longer for settlement or fall back to queuing the new prompt as pending until the worker goes idle.

But there's a second concurrency wrinkle: provider-initiated turns (like Codex's providerTurnActive, or Claude's task-notification turns) can also absorb a mid-flight prompt, and I'm not confident the adapter always resolves that absorbed prompt cleanly. The more robust fix might actually be a watchdog at the bridge/runner level that detects when an ask never resolves and forces resolution rather than relying on the adapter's internal orphan-handling logic.

I wonder if the Claude adapter's internal queue-removal signal for absorbed mid-turn prompts even surfaces over ACP. The real way to verify would be to actually test it against the live bridge: spin up a temp agent via the HTTP API, fire a long prompt, cancel it, then immediately send another and see if it resolves — that's the definitive check, though it costs tokens.

Before running that, I should trace the actual code path first: look at providerTurnActive, provider_turn_ended, runAgentRequest, and how session updates get recorded, to understand where cancellation handling actually happens.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T15:53:53.068Z

I'm tracing the turn timeline: the 15:32:52 result had promptInFlight true, so the steer prompt resolution got skipped, and I'm checking whether it ever got resolved before later task-notification turns ended with results around 15:44-15:47, where provider_turn_ended fired.

So it seems the original prompt's finally clause clobbered the shared promptInFlight flag to false at 15:31:43, even while the steer prompt was still pending on the connection — meaning the steer got absorbed mid-turn into the running original turn rather than starting its own, since it was enqueued at 15:31:35 and marked "absorbed_mid_turn" at 15:31:42.95. That would explain why the original turn kept running until 15:32:52, carrying the steer's content as a mid-turn user message.

I'm now thinking the best way to confirm this is to actually reproduce it: spin up a test agent via the bridge HTTP API, start a long-running prompt, cancel it partway through, then immediately send another prompt right after, and see whether the second one ever resolves — mirroring exactly what happened with the steer. I should check the HTTP routes for creating and cancelling agents to set this up.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T15:56:54.070Z

So the interrupt at 15:31:35.621 cancelled the original turn, but a queued task-notification dequeued right at 15:31:35.628 and started a new turn before our steer prompt even arrived at 15:31:35.712. That means our steer got absorbed mid-turn into the task-notification turn instead, and the adapter's deferred turn for the steer never properly settled.

To reproduce this, I could ask Claude to kick off a background Bash command that finishes in a few seconds while doing something else in the foreground, then cancel right as the background command completes so the notification is queued mid-turn — after cancel it should dequeue immediately and absorb the next prompt. A simpler version: just send a prompt while a task-notification turn is already running, without any cancel involved — have Claude start a background script that takes 5 seconds and end its turn, then see what happens once that notification fires.

So the timing should let the bg notification queue while the build is still running. Then I'll cancel and immediately fire off prompt2 asking something trivial, checking whether it settles within 90 seconds. Before running this, I should clean up the duplicate lines and make the prompts configurable via environment variables.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T16:04:59.696Z

I notice the adapter never settles the absorbed prompt—the first prompt resolved late as "cancelled" right when the notification turn ended, leaving the absorbed second prompt orphaned. I need to figure out where to fix this timing issue.

One option is fixing the adapter itself if the user owns that package locally. Another is adding a watchdog at the OmniHarness bridge level: once a turn result is observed and the prompt stays unsettled after a period of quiet, treat it as settled ourselves—though that risks misfiring if the prompt is legitimately queued behind an unprompted turn.

That's especially risky with long contexts, since time-to-first-token for Opus with hundreds of thousands of tokens could legitimately take 20-30 seconds before thinking blocks start streaming. A false settle wouldn't actually lose the message though, since the bridge already handles unprompted turns and would capture the output as a provider-initiated turn—just less precise than I'd like.

Looking at the old-prompt resolution: the first prompt resolved at the notification-turn end with stopReason cancelled, settling at 47.5s rather than at cancel time (17.5s), which is odd but workable. The deeper issue is that OmniHarness can race with notification turns generally—a user's follow-up can arrive while an unprompted notification turn is active, and since the bridge only reads "working" after the first tool call, there's a window where a prompt gets sent, absorbed at a tool boundary, and orphaned. This seems to be the root cause behind many of the recent cases, so the real fix needs to address that general race rather than just the steer-specific scenario.

The best fix is likely inside the adapter itself, assuming the user owns it — I should check where the adapter source lives, looking at the package.json repository field and any local clone.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T16:13:34.444Z

I realize that message chunk is used for replaying session history, not live state, so I need to fix this at the bridge level with timing-based detection. I also want to add a second guard so cancelAgentTurn doesn't set state to idle while a prompt is in flight, turning promptInFlight into a counter or per-prompt token so concurrent asks don't clobber each other.

I'm thinking about whether to add a runner-side watchdog too, but since the bridge is the authority and fixing it there unblocks the runner's chain, I'll keep the fix there and just have the runner emit/record events defensively. For the manager.askAgent design, I'll use a per-prompt token (a Symbol) stored on the record, clearing promptInFlight only in the finally block if the token still matches the current one -- this way, if a newer prompt was sent after a cancel, the old ask's completion won't incorrectly mark state as idle while the newer one is still running.

Now I'm working through an absorption watchdog: racing the prompt call against a detector that listens for turn-result session updates, resetting a timer on each new session update and re-arming after each turn result, so that if things stay quiet past a grace period after a turn result while the prompt is still unsettled, it settles as absorbed. I'm cross-checking this logic against the third repro case, tracing the timing of the cancelled turn and the subsequent prompt to make sure the detector would actually catch that scenario.

I'm also worried about a false-positive case: if a prompt is sent while a notification turn is running, the real turn's updates might not start until after time-to-first-token, which can be surprisingly long (15s+ in one incident with large context) — so the grace period needs to be generous enough to avoid falsely settling as absorbed, even though such a false settle would be mostly self-healing since the later turn gets handled as unprompted.

I'm looking for a cleaner signal than a timer, like checking turn origin metadata or echo events from the SDK, but neither reliably distinguishes an absorbed human prompt from a genuinely separate turn. Settling on a timer-based approach with maybe a 60s grace period, accepting the tradeoff that a false positive just means a longer visible spinner for the user.

Checking the actual timestamps from the repro logs, the first usage update for a new turn appears roughly 1-1.3s after the prompt is sent, which seems to confirm the adapter emits usage right at turn start rather than waiting for model output.

In another incident, with a large cached context (548k tokens), the gap stretched to about 6.7 seconds between dequeue and first usage report, suggesting a 30-second grace window should be safe even for big prompts. I also need to account for hooks like UserPromptSubmit that might run before the turn officially starts without emitting any usage signal.

For the absorbed-settle case, I'm thinking the response text should just be the accumulated current text, with an end_turn stop reason, and I should emit a named event for prompt absorption carrying the worker ID -- which means adding this new event kind to the named-events union type. The trickier part is handling late resolution: if the underlying prompt promise resolves after we've already settled via absorption, the token guard should prevent it from clobbering state since we clear the active token on absorbed settle, so a mismatched token means no state changes occur, but the original connection.prompt promise itself remains pending.

Even if a late resolution eventually fires, it's a minor memory leak and otherwise harmless. The real concern is if the adapter's off-by-one bookkeeping causes a future prompt to get settled prematurely by an earlier turn's results -- that's less dangerous than hanging, just an early settlement. On the cancel path, since cancelAgentTurn sets state to idle while the old prompt is still in flight, the token guard still protects against the old resolution clobbering the new one, so waiting for the old prompt to settle before sending a new one wouldn't have prevented this particular incident -- skipping that idea.

Looking at promptInFlight semantics in the runtime client, the token approach still works since promptInFlight stays true while a prompt is pending, so settleUnpromptedTurnAtResult gets skipped correctly for absorbed turns. In the normal case, the detector should clear once our own prompt resolves quickly, but I'm now wondering about edge cases where the adapter takes a long time to resolve the prompt -- for instance, if Stop hooks run as part of post-turn processing before the result message is actually emitted, that could delay resolution and trigger the timer unnecessarily.

Given no pending permissions after a result, I need to trace how session updates flow through runtime-client to find where settleUnpromptedTurnAtResult is invoked, so I can hook in a notification to the manager there.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T16:13:47.150Z

I'm trying to figure out what counts as "activity" for resetting the timer, since multiple usage_update events fire right after a result — some with cost, some without, plus origin metadata and rate limit info — and a new turn also starts with a costless usage_update, so I need a cleaner way to distinguish real activity from these trailing bookkeeping updates.

Maybe activity should only reset on non-usage updates like message chunks, thoughts, or tool calls, since a new turn nearly always emits one of those quickly, but if thinking is hidden and the model takes 40+ seconds before producing visible output, that grace window could fail — though the risk feels acceptable given the self-healing behavior where an unprompted turn's first tool call flips state back to working. I should check the runtime-client code for where it sets working state to confirm this happens.

## Claude thinking · 2026-10-06T16:15:20.593Z

I'm realizing a direct follow-up sent while the worker is busy gets a 409 and is handled asynchronously by marking the message delivery as failed, but only logging if not busy — meaning a follow-up during a busy-on-bridge state is silently dropped rather than queued. This is a separate ignored-input path from the steer case: steering requeues when busy, but follow-ups don't, so I need to check whether the frontend compensates for this.

The fix seems clear: when busy, treat the follow-up like the steer branch does — delete the message and recreate it as a queued message with the same clientMessageId, so it drains automatically once the worker goes idle via the existing queue-drain logic on live sync. I still need to verify that deduping works correctly when the queued message is later delivered with the same id, since the stream may have already appended a user_input entry for it.

Now I want to plan the concrete code changes: extending the agent record type with an active prompt token and turn-watch field, wiring watch hooks into the runtime client's session update handler, adding token-guard and absorbed-detection logic in askAgent, keeping cancelAgentTurn mostly as-is since the token guard should handle stale resolutions safely, adding a new named event for prompt absorption, and updating the send-message busy path to requeue instead of dropping. I also want to find existing manager tests using a fake connection so I can model a new unit test for the absorbed-detection behavior.

1	/**
2	 * A Codex /goal starts its next turn by itself, usually before the response to
3	 * the prompt that ran the previous turn reaches us. If `askAgent` then reports
4	 * the agent idle, the runner settles the conversation while the provider keeps
5	 * working, and nothing persists that work (session 9d1e7dd343df lost 8h47m).
6	 */
7	import { afterEach, describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

12	import { __resetNamedEventsForTests } from "@/server/events/named-events";

14	const tempDirs: string[] = [];

23	// Answers a prompt the way codex-acp does when a goal is active: the prompted
24	// turn goes idle, the goal's next turn goes active, then the prompt resolves.
25	const goalContinuationAcpScript = `#!/usr/bin/env node
26	process.stdin.setEncoding('utf8');
27	let buffer = '';
28	
29	function write(message) {
30	  process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(message) + '\\n');
31	}
32	
33	function threadStatus(status) {
34	  write({
35	    jsonrpc: '2.0',
36	    method: 'session/update',
37	    params: {
38	      sessionId: 'session-1',
39	      update: { sessionUpdate: 'session_info_update', _meta: { codex: { threadStatus: status } } },
40	    },
41	  });
42	}
43	
44	process.stdin.on('data', (chunk) => {
45	  buffer += chunk;
46	  const lines = buffer.split(/\\r?\\n/g);
47	  buffer = lines.pop() ?? '';
48	  for (const line of lines) {
49	    if (!line.trim()) continue;
50	    const message = JSON.parse(line);
51	    if (message.method === 'initialize') {
52	      write({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: message.id, result: { protocolVersion: 1 } });
53	    } else if (message.method === 'session/new') {
54	      write({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: message.id, result: { sessionId: 'session-1' } });
55	    } else if (message.method === 'session/prompt') {
56	      threadStatus({ type: 'active', activeFlags: [] });
57	      threadStatus({ type: 'idle' });
58	      threadStatus({ type: 'active', activeFlags: [] });
59	      setTimeout(() => {
60	        write({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: message.id, result: { stopReason: 'end_turn' } });
61	      }, 20);
62	    }
63	  }
64	});
65	
66	process.stdin.on('end', () => process.exit(0));
67	`;
68

I'm sketching a fake ACP script to simulate absorption: the first prompt emits a normal turn with a tool call, message chunk, and cost usage update, while the second (absorbed) prompt emits the notification turn's content—tool call, message, usage update—without ever actually responding, so I can check that askAgent still settles to idle within the configurable grace period.

I also want to test the case where a queued prompt sits behind a notification turn and settles normally once the adapter responds, without triggering an absorbed event. And I want to cover the overlapping-ask scenario where an old prompt resolves (cancelled) after a new one has started, verifying promptInFlight stays true for the new prompt rather than being clobbered by the old one's cleanup logic—worth including since it's cheap and directly tied to the bug. Now I need to check how the manager reads environment config, like the idle timeout setting, to see how options.env is wired in.

      "name": "Bash",
      "description": "Executes a bash command and returns its output.\n\n- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.\n- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.\n- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.\n- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.\n- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.\n\n# Git\n- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.\n- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).\n- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.\n- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.",

Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.\n- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.\n- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.\n- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits.     {
      "name": "ScheduleWakeup",
      "description": "Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.\n\nDo NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.\n\nPass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.\n\nSet `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report (\"no change\", \"still waiting\", \"quiet hold\"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).\n\n## Picking delaySeconds\n\nThis session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)\n\nMatch the delay to what you're actually waiting for:\n\n- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.\n- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.\n- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.\n\nDon't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.\n\n## The reason field\n\nOne short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. \"watching CI run\" beats \"waiting.\" The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.\n",

      "name": "Skill",
      "description": "Invoke a skill.\n\nA skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow).
